fields.h1: Build a Tattoo Consent Form Clients Sign on Their Phones
fields.hero_description: Describe your studio. Emergent builds the tattoo consent form, checks each client's age and photo ID, and saves every signed record to a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What a Tattoo Consent Form Should Record
fields.features_subheading: The client and the design on one signed record, which your front desk can find by name.
fields.feature_1:
Photo ID and date of birth up front

Ask for date of birth before any other question and have the client photograph a government ID. With both on the record, the artist can match the person in the chair to the form.
fields.feature_2:
The design and placement in writing

Describe the piece and where it goes, or attach the final stencil. Your client confirms the size and the spot on the body, and that wording is saved on the record by the signature.
fields.feature_3:
Questions the artist reads first

Ask about latex or pigment allergies and anything else the artist should hear before the stencil goes on. Any yes answer moves that record to the top of the artist's queue.
fields.feature_4:
Aftercare sent with the signed copy

Email each client a PDF of the form they signed, with your studio's aftercare sheet attached. Both pages stay with the client, and the record notes the minute each copy was sent.
fields.feature_5:
One searchable record per session

Save every signed form as a row holding the client, the artist and the date of the session. Type a name at the front desk to see each tattoo that client has had at your studio.
fields.feature_6:
Source code your developer can own

Export the full source to your GitHub when the studio wants consent inside its own booking site. A developer can host the code on any server and keep building on it from there.

fields.tab_content_1:
The flash day line fills from a QR code at the door

Lantern Ink runs a flash day every October. Walk-ins scan a QR code on the door, pick a flash number from the wall and sign while they wait in line. Each signed form posts to the artists' Slack channel with that flash number, and clients are called in signing order. By 3 pm, 31 clients have signed.
fields.tab_content_2:
Sign only after approving the final stencil

Two days before her custom session, Mara Voss gets a link with her final peony design attached. She confirms the size, 6 by 4 inches, and the placement on her left inner forearm. The signature box stays locked until she ticks the design approval. Her artist never starts on a stencil she has not seen.
fields.tab_content_3:
Florida's rule for 16 and 17, checked at booking

Bright Coast Tattoo in Tampa asks for date of birth before anything else. A client who is 16 or 17 gets a parent section with photo ID for both, proof of guardianship and an upload of the notarized state consent form. The booking also notes that the parent must attend. Anyone under 16 cannot book at all.
fields.tab_content_4:
Every guest artist's records, together when the spot ends

Guest artist Theo Lind works a two-week spot at North Pier Tattoo. Each consent form names the artist who did the work, which keeps his 18 sessions apart from the resident artists' records. On his last day, the shop manager exports those 18 signed forms as one PDF, and the originals stay in the studio's table.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Tattoo Consent Form
fields.howto_description: Most of the work is deciding what your artists need to know and who may sign. The fields follow from that.
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Write the questions your artists ask
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Spell out what the client agrees to
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Decide how clients reach the form
fields.howto_step_1_des: Tattoo rules are set state by state, and some counties add their own. Look up the minimum age, what a parent has to bring and which client details your health department expects on file. Florida, for one, wants the client's birthdate and the tattoo's location on every record.
fields.howto_step_2_des: List what an artist asks before starting: pigment or latex allergies, medication that thins the blood, skin conditions near the placement, whether the client has eaten. Each question becomes its own field on the form.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Write the consent in plain sentences. Clients confirm the tattoo is permanent, that the design and placement are final once work starts, and that they will follow the aftercare sheet. Give each statement its own initials box so nobody can say they skimmed it.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Put a link in the booking confirmation for custom work and a printed code by the front window for walk-ins. Keep a tablet at the counter for anyone without a phone. Every entry point opens the same form and saves to the same table of signed records.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Paste your consent wording and list the fields around it. Emergent builds the form with its age check, plus a table of signed records. Ask for changes in plain English, such as a Spanish version or a new question your guest artist wants on every form.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Connect it to the rest of the studio
fields.howto_step_6_des: Post a Slack message when a form is signed, email the client a copy with your aftercare sheet and link each record to its booking. Emergent connects to any tool with an API, including the booking software you already use.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Sign it as a client, then have it read
fields.howto_step_7_des: Fill the form yourself twice, once as a 17-year-old and once as an adult, then open both records. Ask a local attorney to read your consent wording before the first real client signs, because what holds up depends on your state's law.

claims_to_source: Florida allows tattooing a 16- or 17-year-old only when a parent or guardian accompanies them, both show government photo ID, and the parent gives written notarized consent and proof of guardianship; under 16 is not allowed except for medical or dental purposes
Florida tattoo customer records must hold the artist's name, the client's name, age and birthdate, the description and location of the tattoo, both signatures and the date
Florida licenses each tattoo establishment, and an artist's license application must name the licensed establishment where the artist works

Tattoo aftercare: keep it covered as the artist instructs (a few hours or more), avoid soaking it in baths, hot tubs or pools until healed, do not pick scabs, protect it from the sun and wear breathable clothing
A tattoo needle passes through the epidermis into the dermis, which holds nerves and blood vessels, which is why tattooing hurts and the skin bleeds
The 1/3 rule is a design guideline associated with American traditional tattoos: about one third black, one third color and one third bare skin
